The exposed data included 6.8 million unique email addresses, names, physical addresses, purchases and passwords stored as salted MD5 hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In mid-2019, the e-commerce website Storenvy suffered a data breach that exposed millions of customer records. A portion of the breached records were subsequently posted to a hacking forum with cracked password hashes, whilst the entire corpus of 23M rows was put up for sale. The data contained 11M unique email addresses alongside usernames, IP addresses, the user's city, gender date of birth and original salted SHA-1 password hash.

In February 2020, Israeli marketing company Straffic exposed a database with 140GB of personal data. The publicly accessible Elasticsearch database contained over 300M rows with 49M unique email addresses. Exposed data also included names, phone numbers, physical addresses and genders. In their breach disclosure message, Straffic stated that "it is impossible to create a totally immune system, and these things can occur".

In July 2020, the Russian Minecraft service StreamCraft suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data. The data included 1.8M records of usernames, email and IP addresses and passwords stored as either MD5 or bcrypt hashes.

In November 2021, the live sex cams and adult chat website Stripchat left several databases exposed and unsecured. In June the following year, over 10M Stripchat records appeared on a popular hacking forum. The exposed data included usernames, email addresses and IP addresses.

In July 2018, the massive multiplayer online game Stronghold Kingdoms suffered a data breach. Almost 5.2 million accounts were impacted by the incident which exposed emails addresses, usernames and passwords stored as salted SHA-1 hashes.

In October 2025, the publishing platform Substack suffered a data breach that was subsequently circulated more widely in February 2026. The breach exposed 663k account holder records containing email addresses along with publicly visible profile information from Substack accounts, such as publication names and bios. A subset of records also included phone numbers.

In January 2022, the now defunct file upload service Sundry Files suffered a data breach that exposed 274k unique email addresses. The data also included usernames, IP addresses and passwords stored as salted SHA-256 hashes.

In October 2024, the fantasy sports platform SuperDraft suffered a data breach that exposed over 300k customer records. The breach contained 24GB of data including email addresses, usernames, purchases, latitudes and longitudes, dates of birth and bcrypt password hashes.

In February 2021, a series of "free" VPN services were breached including SuperVPN and GeckoVPN, exposing over 20M records. The data appeared together in a single file with a small number of records also included from FlashVPN, suggesting that all three brands may share the same platform. Impacted data also included email addresses, the country logged in from and the date and time each login occurred alongside device information including the make and model, IMSI number and serial number.

In October 2024, the Hungarian IT headhunting service Switch inadvertently exposed thousands of customer records via a public GitHub repository. The exposed data contained job applications with names, email addresses and in some cases, commentary on the applicant.

In February 2024, the paid survey website SurveyLama suffered a data breach that exposed 4.4M customer email addresses. The incident also exposed names, physical and IP addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and passwords stored as either salted SHA-1, bcrypt or argon2 hashes. When contacted about the incident, SurveyLama advised that they had already "notified the users by email".

In June 2020, the Egyptian bus operator Swvl suffered a data breach which impacted over 4 million members of the service. The exposed data included names, email addresses, phone numbers, profile photos, partial credit card data (type and last 4 digits) and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes, all of which was subsequently shared extensively throughout online hacking communities. The data was provided to HIBP by breachbase.pw.

During 2025, the threat-intelligence firm Synthient aggregated 2 billion unique email addresses disclosed in credential-stuffing lists found across multiple malicious internet sources. Comprised of email addresses and passwords from previous data breaches, these lists are used by attackers to compromise other, unrelated accounts of victims who have reused their passwords. The data also included 1.3 billion unique passwords, which are now searchable in Pwned Passwords. Working to turn breached data into awareness, Synthient partnered with HIBP to help victims of cybercrime understand their exposure.

During 2025, Synthient aggregated billions of records of "threat data" from various internet sources. The data contained 183M unique email addresses alongside the websites they were entered into and the passwords used. After normalising and deduplicating the data, 183 million unique email addresses remained, each linked to the website where the credentials were captured, and the password used. This dataset is now searchable in HIBP by email address, password, domain, and the site on which the credentials were entered.

In April 2024, 95k records from the T2 tea store were posted to a popular hacking forum. Data included email and physical addresses, names, phone numbers, dates of birth, purchases and passwords stored as scrypt hashes.

In February 2024, the Australian Telco Tangerine suffered a data breach that exposed over 200k customer records. Attributed to a legacy customer database, the data included physical and email addresses, names, phone numbers and dates of birth. Whilst the Tangerine login process involves sending a one-time password after entering an email address and phone number, it previously used a traditional password which was also exposed as a bcrypt hash.

In November 2019, the Vietnamese education website TaiLieu allegedly suffered a data breach exposing 7.3M customer records. Impacted data included names and usernames, email addresses, dates of birth, genders and passwords stored as unsalted MD5 hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com after being shared on a popular hacking forum. TaiLieu did not respond when contacted about the incident.

In August 2022, the Portuguese airline TAP Air Portugal was the target of a ransomware attack perpetrated by the Ragnar Locker gang who later leaked the compromised data via a public dark web site. Over 5M unique email addresses were exposed alongside other personal data including names, genders, DoBs, phone numbers and physical addresses.

In February 2020, the affiliate marketing network Tamodo suffered a data breach which was subsequently shared on a popular hacking forum. The incident exposed almost 500k accounts including names, email addresses, dates of birth and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Tamodo failed to respond to multiple attempts to report the breach via published communication channels.

In November 2018, the Minecraft modpack platform known as Technic suffered a data breach. Technic promptly disclosed the breach and advised that the impacted data included over 265k unique users' email and IP addresses, chat logs, private messages and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes with a work factor of 13. Technic self-submitted the breach to HIBP.

In April 2020, the custom printed apparel website Teespring suffered a data breach that exposed 8.2 million customer records. The data included email addresses, names, geographic locations and social media IDs.

In March 2025, almost 55k records were breached from the Hungarian education office website TehetségKapu. The data was subsequently published to a popular hacking forum and included email addresses, names and usernames.

In February 2023, the European airport transfers service Terravision suffered a data breach. The breach exposed over 2M records of customer data including names, phone numbers, email addresses, salted password hashes and in some cases, date of birth and country of origin. Terravision did not respond to multiple attempts by individuals period over a period of months to report the incident.

In May 2024, the American luxury retailer Neiman Marcus suffered a data breach which was later posted to a popular hacking forum. The data included 31M unique email addresses, names, phone numbers, dates of birth, physical addresses and partial credit card data (note: this is insufficient to make purchases). The breach was traced back to a series of attacks against the Snowflake cloud service which impacted 165 organisations worldwide.

In October 2024, The Club Penguin Experience (TCPE) suffered a data breach. The incident exposed over 6k subscribers' email addresses alongside usernames, age groups, passwords stored as bcrypt hashes and in some cases, plain text password hints. TCPE sent prompt disclosure notices to impacted customers following the breach.

In September 2019, the Halloween costume store The Halloween Spot suffered a data breach. Originally misattributed to fancy dress store Smiffys, the breach contained 13GB of data with over 10k unique email addresses alongside names, physical and IP addresses, phone numbers and order histories. The Halloween Spot advised customers the breach was traced back to "an old shipping information database".

In July 2024, hacktivists published almost 2GB of data taken from The Heritage Foundation and their media arm, The Daily Signal. The data contained 72k unique email addresses, primarily used for commenting on articles (along with names, IP addresses and the comments left) and by content contributors (along with usernames and passwords stored as either MD5 or phpass hashes).

In February 2023, The Kodi Foundation suffered a data breach that exposed more than 400k user records. Attributed to an account belonging to "a trusted but currently inactive member of the forum admin team", the breach involved the administrator account creating a database backup that was subsequently downloaded before being sold on a hacking forum. The breach exposed email and IP addresses, usernames, genders and passwords stored as MyBB salted hashes. The Kodi Foundation elected to self-submit impacted email addresses to HIBP.

In May 2024, the conservative news website The Post Millennial suffered a data breach. The breach resulted in the defacement of the website and links posted to 3 different corpuses of data including hundreds of writers and editors (IP, physical address and email exposed), tens of thousands of subscribers to the site (name, email, username, phone and plain text password exposed), and tens of millions of email addresses from thousands of mailing lists alleged to have been used by The Post Millennial (this has not been independently verified). The mailing lists appear to be sourced from various campaigns not necessarily run by The Post Millennial and contain a variety of different personal attributes including name, phone and physical address (depending on the campaign). The data was subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum and extensively torrented.

In November 2024, the online course founded by Andrew Tate known as "The Real World" (previously "Hustler's University" suffered a data breach that exposed almost 325k users of the platform. The impacted data was limited to usernames, email addresses and chat logs.

In February 2023, the grad school admissions search website TheGradCafe suffered a data breach that disclosed the personal records of 310k users. The data included email addresses, names and usernames, genders, geographic locations and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Some records also included physical address, phone number and date of birth. TheGradCafe did not respond to multiple attempts to disclose the breach.

In January 2025, the Rezeptwelt (German for "recipe world") forum for Thermomix owners suffered a data breach. The incident exposed 3.1M registered users' details including names, email and physical addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and bios (usually cooking related).

In June 2025, 107k unique customer email addresses were allegedly obtained from TheSqua.re, the "easiest way to find your next serviced apartment". The data also included names, phone numbers and cities which were subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum. TheSqua.re did not respond to repeated attempts to disclose the incident, however multiple impacted HIBP subscribers confirmed the legitimacy and accuracy of the data.

In October 2021, a database backup taken from the 3D model sharing service Thingiverse began extensively circulating within the hacking community. Dating back to October 2020, the 36GB file contained 228 thousand unique email addresses, mostly alongside comments left on 3D models. The data also included usernames, IP addresses, full names and passwords stored as either unsalted SHA-1 or bcrypt hashes. In some cases, physical addresses was also exposed. Thingiverse's owner, MakerBot, is aware of the incident but at the time of writing, is yet to issue a disclosure statement. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In November 2024, the German electricity provider Tibber suffered a data breach that exposed the personal information of 50k customers. The data included names, email addresses, geographic locations (city and postcode) and total spend on purchases.

In August 2020, the Dutch ticketing service Ticketcounter inadvertently published a database backup to a publicly accessible location where it was then found and downloaded in February 2021. The data contained 1.9M unique email addresses which were offered for sale on a hacking forum and in some cases included names, physical and IP addresses, genders, dates of birth, payment histories and bank account numbers. Ticketcounter was later held to ransom with the threat of the breached being released publicly.

In May 2024, the Australian event ticketing company Ticketek reported a data breach linked to a third party cloud-based platform. The following month, the data appeared for sale on a popular hacking forum and was later linked to a series of breaches of the Snowflake cloud storage service. The data contained almost 30M rows with 17.6M unique email addresses alongside names, genders, dates of birth and hashed passwords.

In May 2018, the website for the ticket distribution service Ticketfly was defaced by an attacker and was subsequently taken offline. The attacker allegedly requested a ransom to share details of the vulnerability with Ticketfly but did not receive a reply and subsequently posted the breached data online to a publicly accessible location. The data included over 26 million unique email addresses along with names, physical addresses and phone numbers. Whilst there were no passwords in the publicly leaked data, Ticketfly later issued an incident update and stated that "It is possible, however, that hashed values of password credentials could have been accessed".

In Mid-2023, 300GB of data containing over 100M records from the Chinese video chat platform "Tigo" dating back to March that year was discovered. The data contained over 700k unique names, usernames, email and IP addresses, genders, profile photos and private messages. Tigo did not respond to multiple attempts to disclose the incident.

In late October 2025, data breached from the Hungarian political party TISZA was published online before being extensively redistributed. Stemming from a compromise of the TISZA Világ service earlier in the month, the breach exposed 200k records of personal data including email addresses along with names, phone numbers and physical addresses.

In June 2022, the adult website TNAFlix suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data. The data included 1.4M records of email and IP addresses, usernames and plain text passwords.

In April 2020, Indonesia's largest online store Tokopedia suffered a data breach. The incident resulted in 15M rows of data being posted to a popular hacking forum. An additional 76M rows were later provided to HIBP in July 2020. In total, the data included over 71M unique email addresses alongside names, genders, birth dates and passwords stored as SHA2-384 hashes.

In August 2019, the comic strip creation website ToonDoo suffered a data breach. The data was subsequently redistributed on a popular hacking forum in November where the personal information of over 6M subscribers was shared. Impacted data included email and IP addresses, usernames, genders, the location of the individual and salted password hashes.

In October 2023, the Japanese consultancy firm Toumei suffered a data breach. The breach exposed over 100M lines and 10GB of data including 77k unique email addresses along with names, phone numbers and physical addresses.

In February 2026, the online gaming community Toy Battles suffered a data breach. The incident exposed 1k unique email addresses alongside usernames, IP addresses and chat logs. Following the breach, Toy Battles self-submitted the data to Have I Been Pwned.

In August 2024, a slew of security vulnerabilities were identified with a conglomerate of online services which included the GPS tracking service Tracki. Multiple vulnerabilities exposed the personal records of 372k users of the service including names and email addresses.

In September 2022, the in-game trading marketplace Traderie suffered a data breach that exposed almost 400k records (this preceded a subsequent breach the following year). The incident exposed email and IP addresses, usernames and links to social media profiles.

In December 2020, the Oklahoma state Tourism and Recreation Department suffered a data breach. The incident exposed 637k email addresses across a variety of tables including age ranges against brochure orders and dates of birth against contest entries. Genders, names and physical addresses were also exposed.

In November 2021, the Indonesian real estate website Travelio suffered a data breach that exposed over 470k customer accounts. The data included email addresses, names, password hashes, phone numbers and for some accounts, dates of birth, physical address and Facebook auth tokens.

In January 2024, data was scraped from Trello and posted for sale on a popular hacking forum. Containing over 15M email addresses, names and usernames, the data was obtained by enumerating a publicly accessible resource using email addresses from previous breach corpuses. Trello advised that no unauthorised access had occurred.

In June 2018, the command and control server of a malicious botnet known as the "Trik Spam Botnet" was misconfigured such that it exposed the email addresses of more than 43 million people. The researchers who discovered the exposed Russian server believe the list of addresses was used to distribute various malware strains via malspam campaigns (emails designed to deliver malware).

In March 2025, a phishing attack successfully gained access to Troy Hunt's Mailchimp account and automatically exported a list of people who had subscribed to the newsletter for his personal blog. The exported list contained 16k email addresses and other data automatically collected by Mailchimp including IP address and a derived latitude, longitude and time zone.

In February 2020, the guitar tuition website TrueFire suffered a data breach which impacted 600k members. The breach exposed extensive personal information including names, email and physical addresses, account balances and unsalted MD5 password hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In 2019, the public records search service TruthFinder suffered a data breach that later came to light in early 2023. The data included over 8M unique customer email addresses, names, phone numbers and passwords stored as scrypt hashes.

In January 2022, a vulnerability in Twitter's platform allowed an attacker to build a database of the email addresses and phone numbers of millions of users of the social platform. In a disclosure notice later shared in August 2022, Twitter advised that the vulnerability was related to a bug introduced in June 2021 and that they are directly notifying impacted customers. The impacted data included either email address or phone number alongside other public information including the username, display name, bio, location and profile photo. The data included 6.7M unique email addresses across both active and suspended accounts, the latter appearing in a separate list of 1.4M addresses.

In early 2023, over 200M records scraped from Twitter appeared on a popular hacking forum. The data was obtained sometime in 2021 by abusing an API that enabled email addresses to be resolved to Twitter profiles. The subsequent results were then composed into a corpus of data containing email addresses alongside public Twitter profile information including names, usernames and follower counts.

In May 2025, the South American mobility services platform Ualabee had hundreds of thousands of records scraped from an interface on their platform. The data included 472k unique email addresses along with names, profile photos, dates of birth and phone numbers.

In July 2024, 700k unique email addresses from the audiobook platform Ubook were posted to a popular hacking forum. Allegedly scraped from the service, the data appears to be sourced from the Ubook Exchange (UBX) and also includes names, genders, dates of birth and links to profile photos.

In January 2020, the travel app creator Ulmon suffered a data breach. The service had almost 1.3M records with 777k unique email addresses, names, passwords stored as bcrypt hashes and in some cases, social media profile IDs, telephone numbers and bios. The data was subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum.

In November 2025, the Everest ransomware group claimed Under Armour as a victim and attempted to extort a ransom, alleging they had obtained access to 343GB of data. In January 2026, customer data from the incident was published publicly on a popular hacking forum, including 72M email addresses. Many records also contained additional personal information such as names, dates of birth, genders, geographic locations and purchase information.

In August 2020, the Neapolitan public transport website Unico Campania was hacked and the data extensively circulated. The breach contained 166k user records with email addresses and plain text passwords.

In December 2019, the now defunct gaming website Unigame (maker of Hunter Online) suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data. The data included 844k email addresses and salted MD5 password hashes.

In approximately November 2019, the Russian "Remote preparatory faculty for IT specialties" Universarium suffered a data breach. The incident exposed 565k email addresses and passwords in plain text. Universarium did not respond to multiple attempts to make contact over a period of many weeks. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In December 2020, the University of California suffered a data breach due to vulnerability in in a third-party provider, Accellion. The breach exposed extensive personal data on both students and staff including 547 thousand unique email addresses, names, dates of birth, genders, social security numbers, ethnicities and other academic related data attributes. Further analysis is available in Exploring the Impact of the UC Data Breach. The data was provided to HIBP courtesy of Cyril Gorlla.

In October 2025, the University of Pennsylvania was the victim of a data breach followed by a ransom demand, largely affecting its donor database. After the incident, the attackers sent inflammatory emails to some victims. The data was later published online in February 2026 and included 624k unique email addresses alongside names and physical addresses. For some donor records, additional personal information was exposed, including gender and date of birth. A small subset of records also contained religion, spouse name, estimated income and donation history.

In January 2021, over 11M unique email addresses were discovered by Night Lion Security alongside an extensive amount of personal information including names, physical and IP addresses, phone numbers and dates of birth. Some records also contained social security numbers, driver's license details, personal financial information and health-related data, depending on where the information was sourced from. Initially attributed to Astoria Company, they subsequently investigated the incident and confirmed the data did not originate from their services.

In April 2021, Indian brokerage firm Upstox suffered a data breach. The incident exposed extensive personal information on over 100k customers including names, genders, dates of birth, physical addresses, banking information and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Extensive "know your customer" information was also exposed including scans of bank statements, cheques and identity documents complete with Aadhaar numbers.

In July 2020, the Utah Gun Exchange website suffered a data breach which included several other associated websites. In total, 235k unique email addresses were exposed before being traded online alongside names, usernames, genders, IP addresses and password hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by breachbase.pw.

In August 2020, news broke of a data breach of Russian airline Utair that dated back to the previous year. The breach contained over 400k unique email addresses along with extensive personal information including names, physical addresses, dates of birth, passport numbers and loyalty program details.

In June 2020, the Brazilian fund raising service Vakinha suffered a data breach which impacted almost 4.8 million members. The exposed data included email addresses, names, phone numbers, geographic locations and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes, all of which was subsequently shared extensively throughout online hacking communities. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In October 2020, the Finnish psychotherapy service Vastaamo was the subject of a ransomware attack targeting first the company itself, followed by their patients directly. The original security incident dates back to a period between late 2018 and early 2019 and exposed data including 30k unique email addresses, names, social security numbers and notes on individuals' psychotherapy sessions. This breach has been flagged as "sensitive" and is only searchable by owners of the email addresses and domains exposed in the incident.

In mid-2019, the Indian interactive online tutoring platform Vedantu suffered a data breach which exposed the personal data of 687k users. The JSON formatted database dump exposed extensive personal information including email and IP address, names, phone numbers, genders and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. When contacted about the incident, Vedantu advised that they were aware of the breach and were in the process of informing their customers.

In February 2019, the email address validation service verifications.io suffered a data breach. Discovered by Bob Diachenko and Vinny Troia, the breach was due to the data being stored in a MongoDB instance left publicly facing without a password and resulted in 763 million unique email addresses being exposed. Many records within the data also included additional personal attributes such as names, phone numbers, IP addresses, dates of birth and genders. No passwords were included in the data. The Verifications.io website went offline during the disclosure process, although an archived copy remains viewable.

In April 2020, the Nepalese internet service provider Vianet suffered a data breach. The attack on the ISP led to the exposure of 177k customer records including 94k unique email addresses. Also exposed were names, phone numbers and physical addresses.

In October 2025, data stolen from the Salesforce instances of multiple companies by a hacking group calling itself "Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters" was publicly released. Among the affected organisations was Vietnam Airlines, which had 7.3M unique customer email addresses exposed following a breach of its Salesforce environment in June of that year. The compromised data also included names, phone numbers, dates of birth, and loyalty program membership numbers.

In October 2018, the Russian Minecraft service VimeWorld suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data. The data included 3.1M records of usernames, email and IP addresses and passwords stored as either MD5 or bcrypt hashes.

In March 2022, the now defunct Colombian airline Viva Air suffered a data breach and subsequent ransomware attack. Among a trove of other ransomed data, the incident exposed a log of 2.6M transactions with 932k unique email addresses, physical and IP addresses, names, phone numbers and partial credit card data (last 4 digits).

In June 2019, the hacking website Void.to suffered a data breach. There were 95k unique email addresses spread across 86k forum users and other tables in the database. A rival hacking website claimed responsibility for breaching the MyBB based forum which disclosed email and IP addresses, usernames, private messages and passwords stored as either salted MD5 or bcrypt hashes.

In March 2023, the "AI-first global cloud platform" Vultr disclosed a security incident at a third-party vendor. Dating back to the previous year, the incident was attributed to the ActiveCampaign email marketing service provider and resulted in the exposure of 188k unique email addresses. A small number of records also included name, IP address and country of origin. No Vultr systems or additional customer data were impacted. Vultr subsequently self-submitted the impacted data to HIBP.

In August 2022, the European streaming service Wakanim suffered a data breach which was subsequently advertised and sold on a popular hacking forum. The breach exposed 6.7M customer records including email, IP and physical addresses, names and usernames.

In approximately December 2018, the digital mall Wanelo suffered a data breach. The data was later placed up for sale on a dark web marketplace along with a collection of other data breaches in April 2019. A total of 23 million unique email addresses were included in the breach alongside passwords stored as either MD5 or bcrypt hashes. After the initial HIBP load, further data containing names, shipping addresses and IP addresses were also provided to HIBP, albeit without direct association to the email addresses and passwords.

In June 2023, the Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department announced a data breach of their Washington State Food Worker Card online training system. The breach was published to a popular hacking forum the year before and dated back to a 2018 database backup. Included in the data were 1.6M unique email addresses along with names, post codes, dates of birth and approximately 9.5k driver's licence numbers.

In June 2020, the user-generated stories website Wattpad suffered a huge data breach that exposed almost 270 million records. The data was initially sold then published on a public hacking forum where it was broadly shared. The incident exposed extensive personal information including names and usernames, email and IP addresses, genders, birth dates and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes.

In January 2021, the Indian wedding planning platform WedMeGood suffered a data breach that exposed 1.3 million customers. The breach exposed 41.5GB of data including email and physical addresses, names, genders, phone numbers and password hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In February 2023, data belonging to the Asian and Hispanic food delivery service Weee appeared on a popular hacking forum. Dating back to mid-2022, the data included 1.1M unique email addresses from 11M rows of orders containing names, phone numbers and delivery instructions.

In March 2021, the Stripe account of the now-defunct WeLeakInfo service was taken over by "pompompurin" after acquiring an expired domain name with an email address used to manage the account. Access to Stripe then exposed almost 12k unique email addresses from customers who'd made credit card payments in order to obtain breached data hosted by WeLeakInfo. The data was subsequently leaked publicly and also included names, payment histories, IP addresses, billing addresses, partial credit card data and the organisation making the purchase.
LINDDUN categories: Linkability, Identifiability, Disclosure of information, Non-compliance

Description: In late 2023, the Dutch appliance store Welhof suffered a data breach. The incident exposed over 100k unique email addresses along with names, physical addresses and the value of purchases made.

In December 2025, the dating website "for a Europid vision" WhiteDate suffered a data breach that was subsequently leaked online, initially exposing 6.1k unique email addresses. The leaked data included extensive personal information such as physical appearance, income, education and IQ. A more comprehensive dataset was later provided to HIBP, containing usernames, IP addresses, private messages, phpBB password hashes and a total of 20k unique email addresses.
LINDDUN categories: Linkability, Identifiability, Detectability, Disclosure of information, Non-compliance

Description: In June 2019, the library of Vienna (Wiener Büchereien) suffered a data breach. The compromised data included 224k unique email addresses, names, physical addresses, phone numbers and dates of birth. The breached data was subsequently posted to Twitter by the alleged perpetrator of the breach.

In October 2018, the site dedicated to posting naked photos and other erotica of wives Wife Lovers suffered a data breach. The underlying database supported a total of 8 different adult websites and contained over 1.2M unique email addresses. Wife Lovers acknowledged the breach which impacted names, usernames, email and IP addresses and passwords hashed using the weak DEScrypt algorithm. The breach has been marked as "sensitive" due to the nature of the site.

In December 2025, 2.3M records of WIRED magazine users allegedly obtained from parent company Condé Nast were published online. The most recent data dated back to the previous September and exposed email addresses and display names, as well as, for a small number of users, their name, phone number, date of birth, gender, and geographic location or full physical address. The WIRED data allegedly represents a subset of Condé Nast brands the hacker also claims to have obtained.

In May 2022, the now defunct social media influencer platform WiredBucks suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data. The incident exposed over 900k email and IP addresses alongside names, usernames, earnings via the platform, physical addresses and passwords stored as plain text.

In January 2020, the mobile app to "compare anything" Wishbone suffered another data breach which followed their breach from 2016. An extensive amount of personal information including almost 10M unique email addresses alongside names, phone numbers geographic locations and other personal attributes were leaked online and extensively redistributed. Passwords stored as unsalted MD5 hashes were also included in the breach.

In July 2020, the French e-commerce platform WiziShop suffered a data breach. The breach exposed 18GB worth of data including names, phone numbers, dates of birth, physical and IP addresses, SHA-1 password hashes and almost 3 million unique email addresses.

In October 2020, 17 previously undisclosed data breaches appeared for sale including the Thai restaurant, hotel and attraction finding service, Wongnai. The breach exposed almost 4M unique customer records from some time during 2020 along with names, phone numbers, links to social media profiles and passwords stored as MD5 hashes. The data was self-submitted to HIBP by Wongnai.

In March 2024, WoTLabs (World of Tanks Statistics and Resources) suffered a data breach and website defacement attributed to "chromebook breachers". The breach exposed 22k forum members' personal data including email and IP addresses, usernames, dates of birth and time zones.

In November 2018, the WordPress sandboxing service that allows people to create temporary websites WP Sandbox discovered their service was being used to host a phishing site attempting to collect Microsoft OneDrive accounts. After identifying the malicious site, WP Sandbox took it offline, contacted the 858 people who provided information to it then self-submitted their addresses to HIBP. The phishing page requested both email addresses and passwords.

In July 2019, the forum for webcomic XKCD suffered a data breach that impacted 562k subscribers. The breached phpBB forum leaked usernames, email and IP addresses and passwords stored in MD5 phpBB3 format. The data was provided to HIBP by white hat security researcher and data analyst Adam Davies.

In November 2024, data from the Senegalese payment platform Yonéma was posted to a popular hacking forum. The data included 36k unique email addresses alongside phone numbers, names and what appears to be encrypted passwords and dates of birth.

In June 2020, the Mexican lending platform yotepresto.com suffered a data breach. Over 1.4 million customers were impacted by the breach which disclosed email and IP addresses, usernames and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In December 2024, data claimed to be breached from the multi-level marketing company Young Living Essential Oils was posted to a popular hacking forum. The data contained 1.1M unique email addresses alongside names, the country of the account and in many cases, their date of birth. Young Living Essential Oils did not respond to multiple attempts to contact them about the data.

In February 2019, data from the live broadcasting service YouNow appeared for sale on a dark web marketplace. Whilst it's not clear what date the actual breach occurred on, the impacted data included 18M unique email addresses, IP addresses, names, usernames and links to social media profiles. As authentication is performed via social providers, no passwords were exposed in the breach. Many records didn't have associated email addresses thus the unique number is lower than the reported total number of accounts.

In January 2019, the Indonesian college and career platform Youthmanual suffered a data breach that exposed 1.1M records of data. The breached included 938k unique email addresses along with extensive personal information including names, genders, dates and places of birth, phone numbers, physical addresses and salted SHA-1 password hashes.

In October and November 2018, security researcher Bob Diachenko identified several unprotected MongoDB instances believed to be hosted by a data aggregator. Containing a total of over 66M records, the owner of the data couldn't be identified but it is believed to have been scraped from LinkedIn hence the title "You've Been Scraped". The exposed records included names, both work and personal email addresses, job titles and links to the individuals' LinkedIn profiles.

In December 2022, the investment research company Zacks announced a data breach. The following month, reports emerged of the incident impacting 820k customers. However, in June 2023, a corpus of data with almost 9M Zacks customers appeared before being broadly circulated on a popular hacking forum. The most recent data was dated May 2020 and included names, usernames, email and physical addresses, phone numbers and passwords stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes. On disclosure of the larger breach, Zacks advised that in addition to their original report "the unauthorised third parties also gained access to encrypted [sic] passwords of zacks.com customers, but only in the encrypted [sic] format".

In June 2024, the investment research company Zacks was allegedly breached, and data was later published to a popular hacking forum. This comes after a separate Zacks data breach confirmed by the organisation in 2023 with the subsequent breach disclosing millions of additional records representing a superset of data from the first incident. The 2024 breach included 12M unique email addresses along with IP and physical addresses, names, usernames, phone numbers and unsalted SHA-256 password hashes. Zacks did not respond to multiple attempts to contact them about the incident.

In June 2024, a data brach sourced from French fashion brand Zadig & Voltaire was publicly posted to a popular hacking forum. The data included names, email and physical addresses, phone numbers and genders. When contacted about the incident, Zadig & Voltaire advised the incident had occurred more than 6 months ago and that "all measures were taken quickly".

In November 2021, web host ZAP-Hosting suffered a data breach that exposed over 60GB of data containing 746k unique email addresses. The breach also contained support chat logs, IP addresses, names, purchases, physical addresses and phone numbers.

In November 2025, data breached from the Zilvia.net Nissan 240SX Silvia and Z Fairlady car forum was leaked. The breach exposed 288k unique email addresses along with usernames, IP addresses and salted MD5 password hashes sourced from the vBulletin based platform. Attempts to contact Zilvia.net about the incident were unsuccessful.

In June 2024, almost 10M user records from Z-lib were discovered exposed online. Now defunct, Z-lib was a malicious clone of Z-Library, a well-known shadow online platform for pirating books and academic papers. The exposed data included usernames, email addresses, countries of residence, Bitcoin and Monero cryptocurrency wallet addresses, purchases and bcrypt password hashes.

In July 2018, the Indian self-drive car rental company Zoomcar suffered a data breach which was subsequently sold on a dark web marketplace in 2020. The breach exposed over 3.5M records including names, email and IP addresses, phone numbers and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In January 2020, the online dating service Zoosk suffered a data breach which was subsequently shared extensively across online hacking communities. The breach contained 24 million unique email addresses alongside extensive personal information including genders, sexualities, dates of birth, physical attributes such as height and weight, religions, ethnicities and political views. The breach also allegedly exposed MD5 password hashes, although the data circulating in hacking circles had this field nulled out. The breach was provided to HIBP by breachbase.pw.
LINDDUN categories: Linkability, Identifiability, Disclosure of information, Non-compliance

Description: In 2024, the 40+ dating website Senior Dating suffered a data breach. Attributed to an exposed Firebase database, the breach included extensive personal information on 766k users of the service including email addresses, photos, genders, links to Facebook accounts, dates of birth and precise latitude and longitude, among other personal attributes. The website was shut down after the breach was acknowledged by the site operator in December, along with a breach of the "ladies.com" website run by the same organisation.
LINDDUN categories: Linkability, Identifiability, Disclosure of information, Non-compliance

Description: In January 2023, the Japanese arm of Zurich insurance suffered a data breach that exposed 2.6M customer records with over 756k unique email addresses. The data was subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum and also included names, genders, dates of birth and details of insured vehicles.

In September 2019, game developer Zynga (the creator of Words with Friends) suffered a data breach. The incident exposed 173M unique email addresses alongside usernames and passwords stored as salted SHA-1 hashes. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

In April 2022, Russian pharmaceutical company Gemotest suffered a data breach that exposed 31 million patients. The data contained 6.3 million unique email addresses along with names, physical addresses, dates of birth, passport and insurance numbers. Gemotest was later fined for the breach.
LINDDUN categories: Linkability, Identifiability, Disclosure of information, Non-compliance

Description: In March 2020, the Korean interior decoration website ???? (Decorating the House) suffered a data breach which impacted almost 1.3 million members. Served via the URL ggumim.co.kr, the exposed data included email addresses, names, usernames and phone numbers, all of which was subsequently shared extensively throughout online hacking communities. The data was provided to HIBP by breachbase.pw.

In April 2024, a substantial volume of data was taken from the Bangladeshi IT services provider Tappware and published to a popular hacking forum. Comprising of 95k unique email addresses, the data also included extensive labour information on local citizens including names, physical addresses, job titles, dates of birth, genders and scans of government issued national identity (NID) cards.

In September 2019, the zoophilia and bestiality forum Zooville suffered a data breach. The usernames and email addresses of 71k members were accessed via an unpatched vulnerability in the vBulletin forum software then subsequently distributed online. A second data set was later provided to HIBP which contained a complete vBulletin database dump including IP addresses, dates of birth and passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. The site administrator advised that following the breach, all data had been deleted from the forum and a new one had been stood up on the XenForo platform.

China-nexus threat cluster UNC6201 exploited zero-day vulnerability CVE-2026-22769 in Dell RecoverPoint for Virtual Machines beginning mid-2024, allowing the threat actors to move laterally, maintain persistent access and deploy malware including SLAYSTYLE, BRICKSTORM and GRIMBOLT. The RecoverPoint software contained a hard-coded credential vulnerability which was exploited remotely, leading to unauthorised access to the underlying operating system and root-level persistence. Dell released a security advisory based on technical reports by Google and Mandiant published on 17 February 2026.

An unknown threat actor launched a DDoS attack on the information and ticketing system of Deutsche Bahn, Germany's largest rail transport company from 17 to 18 February. The incident, which occurred in waves, flooded the company's servers with simultaneous requests, causing them to collapse and resulting in the information and ticket reservation systems being taken out of service for several hours. The attack affected both the DB Navigator mobile app and the official website bahn.de, preventing users from checking schedules, buying tickets, and accessing real-time information about trains. The services were restored by midday on 18 February. According to the head of the German Federal Office for Security in Information Technology (BSI), the risk of a renewed attack remains. The attack was reported by various news outlets on 18 February 2026.

Interlock ransomware group conducted a ransomware attack on Issaqueena Pediatric Dentistry, a South Carolina pediatric dentistry office in the United States, between 9 November 2025 and 11 November 2025. Interlock gained access to certain files within its systems, affecting 501 individuals. The practice informed the public about the attack on its website and submitted the incident to the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Civil Rights Breach Portal on 4 February 2026. The dentistry offered pre-paid identity protection services to affected customers. The practice is working with law enforcement and third-party experts in their ongoing investigation into the incident. Interlock claimed responsibility for the attack and said it had exfiltrated 118 GB of data.

In 2025, VOLTZITE compromised Sierra Wireless Airlink cellular gateways to access U.S. midstream pipeline operations and then pivoted to engineering workstations, manipulating engineering workstation software to extract configuration files and alarm data. The group, which shares technical overlaps with Volt Typhoon, was observed investigating operational conditions that would trigger process shutdowns. Dragos reported the incident on 17 February 2026.

In June 2025, BAUXITE deployed two custom wiper malware variants against Israeli targets during the Iran-Israel conflict, escalating from prior access and disruption to destructive intent. The attackers targeted internet-exposed HMIs, misconfigured engineering workstations, and open field protocols such as Modbus/TCP and DNP3. BAUXITE exhibits technical overlap with activity the U.S. Government assesses is aligned with CyberAv3ngers and IRGC-CEC.  Dragos OT Cybersecurity reported the incident in a report on 17 February 2026.

LockBit targeted the Federal Mortgage Society (SHF) in Mexico on 20 January 2026, disclosing approximately 277 gigabytes of information and setting a payment deadline that expired on 5 February 2026. The attack was carried out by LockBit affiliates who used phishing, abused existing valid accounts, and exploited exposed remote services to gain initial access. The attackers then conducted reconnaissance, executed lateral movement, and exfiltrated information before encrypting systems. The incident was disclosed by LockBit on 21 January 2026.

Title (Company): Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available
Description: On 11 February 2026, Elastic Security Labs published a report outlining how it had observed an ongoing campaign since at least November 2025 by a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group known as UAT8099 or REF4033; the campaign had impacted victims in Australia, Bangladesh, Brazil, China, India, Japan, Korea, Lithuania, Nepal, and Vietnam.  The group was observed deploying BADIIS malware onto Windows web servers and coordinating a large-scale SEO poisoning operation from countries across the globe, impacting over 1800 victims across government agencies, educational institutions, healthcare providers, e-commerce platforms, media outlets, and financial services; Elastic links this to a large-scale, opportunistic effort rather than specifically targeting these entitites. The campaign operates through a two-phase process, first serving keyword-stuffed HTML to search engine crawlers to poison search results, and next, redirecting victims to a sprawling “vice economy” of illicit gambling platforms, pornography, and sophisticated cryptocurrency phishing sites. By deploying the BADIIS malware, a malicious IIS module that integrates directly into a web server's request processing pipeline, the group hijacks the web servers for legitimate government, educational, and corporate domains. This high-reputation infrastructure is used to manipulate search engine rankings, thereby allowing attackers to intercept web traffic and facilitate widespread financial fraud. The malware uses the CopyFileA function to move the contents from the masqueraded files into the .NET directory. Next, the malware parses the DefaultAppPool.config file, examining each node to update the and nodes. The module will inject configuration content from the previously masqueraded file, updating the IIS configuration via a series of append operations. The BADIIS module registers within the request processing pipeline, positioning itself as both the first and the last handler. For each request, the module verifies specific properties and selects an injection or redirection strategy based on the results.
Techniques Used: Content Injection, Exploit Public-Facing Application, Phishing

Title (Company): Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma
Description: On 8 December 2025, the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma were targeted by a ransomware attack, which disrupted tribal systems, including email and phone services. The incident was claimed by the Rhysida ransomware group, although this was not publicly confirmed by the tribes or federal authorities. The incident was reported by the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribal Tribune on 2 January 2026.

On 28 January 2026, the "Choisir le service public" platform, a recruitment and promotion platform for public service jobs, was compromised, resulting in a data breach that affected 377,418 candidates. The stolen information included user identification data, such as first names, full postal addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and email addresses, as well as more sensitive information concerning their career paths and professional aspirations. The breach occurred via the compromise of a management account. The data was put up for sale on the Dark Web, with the information of 1,000 candidates already freely available. The platform disclosed the incident, and it has taken measures to strengthen the security of its systems, notified the relevant authorities, and plans to file a criminal complaint.

On or before 21 January 2026, an unknown threat actor gained unauthorised access to administrative accounts of the Technical University of Vienna in the Active Directory, stealing password hashes in the process. The theft of these password hashes resulted in the Technical University requiring all passwords to be reset. The university detected the incident on 23 January 2026 and informed the data protection authorities on 26 January 2026.

On or around 13 February 2026, the phone systems and network of Livingston HealthCare, a nonprofit hospital in Livingston, Montana, were disrupted by an unknown actor, which further resulted in other systems being brought offline as a precaution. The hospital advised patients with urgent needs to call 911 or go directly to the emergency department. By 16 February 2026, the hospital's phone system had been restored, but some network services remained limited.

At an unknown point on the weekend of 6 February 2026, ShinyHunters stole the data of up to 6.2 million people from Odido, the largest telecommunications provider in the Netherlands. The accessed data included full names, addresses, phone numbers, customer numbers, email addresses, account numbers, date of birth, and passport and drivers license information. The incident involved personal data from a customer contact system used by Odido and was reported to the Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) by Odido. Ben, a subsidiary of Odido, also had data stolen in the course of the breach, as Ben's data was also stored with the system data that was accessed. On 26 February 2026, ShinyHunters leaked two million records of Odido after the company refused to pay the ransom.

On or around 13 February 2026, Figure, a blockchain-based lending firm, was the victim of a data theft by the ShinyHunters cybercrime group. The attack reportedly occurred when an employee was the victim of a social engineering scheme which enabled attackers to steal a "limited amount of data."  ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the breach, listing Figure on its leak site and releasing about 2.5GB of stolen data after no ransom was paid; the stolen and leaked data included names, addresses, birth dates, and phone numbers, though it is unclear if this data belongs to employees, clients, or partners.

Title (Company): Centre Region Council of Governments - Borough of State College, Pennsylvania
Description: On 11 February 2026, the borough of State College, Pennsylvania suffered a cybersecurity attack that disrupted its network. The disruption was linked by the borough to delayed email responses, while the Centre Region Council of Governments, which contracts the borough for cyber services, was also impacted by the breach, forcing it to close until further notice.

Title (Company): U.S. Virgin Islands Economic Development Authority
Description: On or around 12 February 2026, the U.S. Virgin Islands Economic Development Authority was hit by a ransomware attack, which locked its computer systems and included a ransom demand of more than $300,000. The attack was confirmed by Gov. Albert Bryan Jr. in an interview with The Virgin Islands Consortium. The government did not detail which internal applications were affected or whether any public-facing services were disrupted, beyond confirming the systems were locked.

On 10 February 2026, the IT system of the municipality of Nosate (Italy) was the victim of a cyberattack which resulted in the likely exposure of municipal data, though the exact type of data stolen is unclear as of the time of writing (16 February 2026). Nosate officials stated that an investigation was underway to determine what data had been accessed and/or stolen, and officials called for vigilance among the population to report any suspicious communication.

On or around 9 February 2026, the Nippon Medical School Musashi-Kosugi Hospital was hit by a ransomware attack from unknown actors, resulting in the leak of approximately 10,000 patients’ personal information. The attack was carried out by exploiting a vulnerability in a VPN device used for medical equipment maintenance, and the attackers demanded 15 billion yen (roughly US$100 million) in ransom.

Title (Company): City of Frisco - City of Palm Bay - BridgePay Network Solutions
Description: On or around 6 February 2026, unknown threat actors disrupted the services of BridgePay Network Solutions, a payments gateway and solutions provider based in the United States, in a ransomware attack that knocked key payment systems offline, thus disrupting several US-based municipalities' payment services, such as Palm Bay (Florida) and Frisco (Texas). The company contacted federal law enforcement, including the FBI and the U.S. Secret Service, and brought in outside forensic and recovery teams.

On or around 4 February 2026, the Tulare City School District in California was the victim of a ransomware attack by an actor(s) dubbed "SingularityMD." The attack disrupted certain computer systems of the school district, according to a notice published for community members. The attacker(s) reportedly sent extortion-style messages threatening to release student-related records unless a ransom demand was met, though it was unclear as of the time of writing (16 February 2026) what information these records might entail.

On 30 January 2026, the European Commission detected a cyberattack on its mobile device management system; the Commission stated in a press release that the attack may have resulted in attackers accessing some staff data, including names and phone numbers. The Commission reported that it had contained and cleaned the system within nine hours of the attack.

Title (Company): Cortina Hotel - Ministry of Foreign Affairs - Italian Embassy in Washington D.C.
Description: On or around 4 February 2026, a coordinated DDoS attack was launched by the pro-Russian collective NoName057(52) against Italian institutional websites and digital platforms connected to the Milan-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics, including the offices of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Hotels in Cortina d’Ampezzo. The attack aimed to saturate servers and make websites unreachable, but was identified and mostly blocked in its initial phase by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' internal security structures, thereby avoiding prolonged interruptions to services and leaks of sensitive data. However, several websites were successfully disrupted in the course of the attack, including the portals of the Austrian and Finnish Olympic Committees, the German national team, and a restaurant in Cortina. Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani informed the public about the attack on 4 February 2026, stating that the attacks originated from Russia. The timely response prevented escalation and limited the perceived impact on users.

Title (Company): Ivanti Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM) - Valtori - Dutch Data Protection Authority (DPA) - Council for the Judiciary
Description: On or before 29 January 2026, Ivanti Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM) was breached by hackers who exploited two critical zero-day code injection flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-1281 and CVE-2026-1340, which allowed remote code execution. The vulnerabilities, classified as CWE-94, were given a severity score of 9.8 out of 10. WatchTowr researchers discovered that the flaws were being actively exploited by attackers to break into systems and set up digital backdoors by sending specifically crafted requests to trick the system's Bash scripts into running malicious code. Ivanti released an emergency advisory and provided a temporary RPM patch fix on 29 January 2026. The attack was disclosed by watchTowr through their blog post and shared with Hackread.com on 2 February 2026. Several affected organizations reported being breached, including the Dutch Data Protection Agency and Council of Judiciary, and the Finnish national agency Valtori. The European Commission also issued a statement disclosing an intrusion in its “central infrastructure managing mobile devices” without explicitly linking the breach to Ivanti. However, several media reports suggest a connection between the incident affecting the European Commission and the Ivanti breach.

On 19 January 2026, the Directorate of File Automation (DAF) in Senegal was the victim of a data theft by a ransomware group called "Green Blood Group."  Green Blood Group claimed the theft of 139 terabytes of biometric data and sensitive information on immigration and subsequently leaked samples of the data, including an email from a senior general manager at a Malaysian company tasked with creating Senegal’s new digital identification cards.  The senior general manager of the Malaysian company informed the DAF on 20 January that the hackers had breached two DAF servers, and the DAF's operations (e.g., ID creation) were reportedly disrupted as a result of the incident response, with systems belonging to the DAF being shut down as a precaution to prevent further damage of the 19 January incident. As of the time of writing (10 February 2026), the website of the DAF is inaccessible.

In the Norwegian Police Security Services' (PST) 2026 Annual National Threat Assessment, published in February 2026, the Norwegian government confirmed that the Chinese state-sponsored APT group Salt Typhoon compromised network devices in multiple Norwegian organisations at an unspecified time in 2025. While specifics of the incident(s) were not clarified outside of the fact that Salt Typhoon had in fact compromised Norwegian organisations, Beate Gangås, the Director General of the PST, described increasing pressure from multiple foreign intelligence services, particularly China, Russia, and Iran and said that Norway was facing its "most serious security threat since World War II."

The Russian Qilin Ransomware Group breached Romania's national oil pipeline operator Conpet, on 3 February 2026, disrupting parts of its IT infrastructure and its website. The Qilin Ransomware Group claimed responsibility for the incident, stating they had stolen nearly one terabyte of data, including internal documents, financial records and passport scans, which were published on their dark web leak site on 5 February 2026. Conpet's operational technology systems, including SCADA and telecommunications systems, remained fully functional and oil transport operations were not affected. The company's specialists took immediate steps to mitigate the impact and an investigation was launched in collaboration with Romania's national cybersecurity authorities. Conpet also filed a criminal complaint.  Conpet reported the incident to the public in a statement on 4 February 2026.

Unattributed perpetrators breached Gozo Channel, a Maltese ferry operator, on 3 February 2026, which disrupted its internal IT systems. Ferry operations were not affected and services continued according to the standard timetable. The company stated that the incident was contained promptly due to IT infrastructure and established contingency measures. Technical teams worked to restore administrative systems.

Unidentified hackers deployed ransomware against the City of New Britain, Connecticut on 29 January 2026, disrupting city network systems for more than 48 hours. The attack began early Wednesday morning when the New Britain Police Department was notified of a network disruption that spread throughout the city's internet server. The city confirmed that the internet went down at around 5 a.m. Police and fire department networks were affected, but emergency operations remained functional due to backup plans and manual redundancy measures. Essential services including road maintenance, trash collection and utilities continued. The city engaged cybersecurity experts and worked with the FBI and state and federal authorities to investigate. At the time of reporting, it was unclear whether personal or confidential information stored on the city's server was impacted.

Unknown threat actors deployed ransomware against Sapienza University of Rome on 2 February 2026, encrypting systems and blocking access to the university's website, internal networks and administrative services. The attackers imposed a 72-hour deadline for ransom payment in cryptocurrency. The university ordered the immediate blocking of network systems and engaged the Italian National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) to support cleanup operations. Backup systems isolated from the main network were not affected, enabling restoration without payment. The Rome Public Prosecutor's Office opened an investigation. The university announced on 5 February 2026 that services would be gradually restored.

Title (Company): Government entities and law enforcement agencies - Government entities and law enforcement agencies - Government entities and law enforcement agencies - Government entities and law enforcement agencies - Government entities and law enforcement agencies - Government entities and law enforcement agencies
Description: Chinese state-linked group Amaranth-Dragon conducted cyberespionage campaigns targeting government and law enforcement agencies across Southeast Asia from March 2025 to October 2025. Check Point Research published findings on 4 February 2026, assessing that the group's tools and techniques overlap with APT-41, suggesting a connection or shared resources. The campaigns targeted entities in Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines, with attack themes coinciding with significant local geopolitical events. Beginning in August 2025, the group exploited a newly disclosed path traversal vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2025-8088) to achieve code execution and persistence on victim systems. The vulnerability was disclosed on 8 August 2025; Amaranth-Dragon weaponised it by 18 August 2025. The threat actors distributed malicious RAR archives via spearphishing emails, often hosted on legitimate services such as Dropbox. The archives contained a custom loader dubbed Amaranth Loader, which retrieved AES-encrypted payloads and deployed the Havoc command-and-control framework.

Title (Company): Unspecified Government Officials and International Diplomats  - Unspecified Government Officials and International Diplomats
Description: Chinese state-sponsored group Mustang Panda (also known as HoneyMyte) targeted government officials and international diplomats across Asia and Eastern Europe with a cyberespionage campaign between late December 2025 and mid-January 2026. Security researchers at Dream identified the campaign and shared their findings with Hackread.com on 4 February 2026.The threat actors distributed spearphishing emails masquerading as official US diplomatic correspondence, with subject lines referencing policy updates or internal briefings. The emails contained malicious PDF documents designed to appear as authoritative summaries typically shared by the United States after high-level meetings. Opening the file was sufficient to trigger the compromise. The attackers deployed DOPLUGS, a downloader variant of the PlugX surveillance tool, using DLL search-order hijacking and custom encryption routines to evade detection. The malware used PowerShell to deploy additional tools for data collection.Dream Research Labs first detected the threat in mid-January 2026 after an AI-based hunting agent flagged a suspicious archive. Researchers assessed that the campaign targeted individuals involved in elections and international coordination.
Techniques Used: Drive-by Compromise, Phishing, Replication Through Removable Media

Description: On or around 2 February 2026, a cyber attack was carried out by a threat actor/group known as HaciendaSec, who claimed to have hacked into the Spanish Ministry of Finance's database and accessed the private data of over 47 million Spanish citizens. The attacker allegedly stole sensitive information, including ID numbers, full names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, IBAN numbers, and tax payment details. The data was put up for sale on a dark web forum and sample data was published as evidence of the theft.

Title (Company): Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities
Description: On or around 2 February 2026, an individual known under the alias "Gordon Freeman," allegedly breached the website of the Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities by exploiting an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability combined with leaked credentials. The attacker listed the Ministry on a leak site and claimed to have obtained identity documents, bank account numbers, and other sensitive data, including copies of ID cards, passports, university degrees, academic certificates, proof of enrolment, study plans, email addresses, and bank details, affecting workers and university students; however, the Ministry had not released a public statement or confirmation as of 4 February 2026.

On 28 January 2026, ShinyHunters claimed it carried out a cyberattack on the Match Group, the company behind popular dating apps including Tinder, Hinge, and OkCupid, by using a voice phishing (vishing) technique to gain initial access through Okta's corporate authentication system.  The attackers claimed to have stolen approximately 1.7GB of compressed data, comprising internal documents, company receipts, and unique advertising identifiers associated with some users. Match Group confirmed the incident on 30 January 2026 and stated that it had blocked unauthorised access and launched an investigation with external cybersecurity experts.

On 31 January 2026, the X account of the chief of the Bangladeshi political party Jamaat-e-Islami, Shafiqur Rahman, was allegedly hacked by unknown attackers using malware to briefly gain control of the account and disseminate false and unauthorised statements.  The attack occurred between 4:37pm and 5:09pm, during which time the hackers logged in from another location without changing the account password. Jamaat-e-Islami's cyber team later regained control using existing security protocols. The party alleged that the attackers used a government email address to hack the account. Following the incident, Sirajul Islam, a member of Jamaat-e-Islami's National Election Steering Committee, filed a general diary (GD) at Hatirjheel Police Station in Dhaka on 01 February 2026. The party claimed that the name of the individual and the email address used in the incident are available on a government website. The attack was reported by Jamaat-e-Islami's central publicity department in a statement issued shortly after midnight on 01 February 2026.

On 26 January 2026, unknown threat actors carried out a "large-scale, well-organized and coordinated" cyber attack that disrupted the systems of "Delta," a Russian anti-theft security systems manufacturer, leading to security systems and cars malfunctioning across Russia, with some cars locking and/or stopping entirely, even while driving. While Delta denied the theft of data, an unidentified Telegram channel claimed it had published an archive of stolen data, though the authenticity of the data could not be confirmed; Delta stated only that an unspecified "hostile country" was behind the attack.

On 31 January 2026, Step Finance, a Solana-based platform, was breached resulting in the theft of approximately $27 million to $30 million worth of assets. The attackers exploited a known vulnerability in the infrastructure, compromising several treasury wallets and triggering a sharp decline in the project's native token, STEP, which plummeted by over 90 percent. Step Finance reported that around 261,854 Solana (SOL) were withdrawn and transferred from wallets controlled by the platform. The incident was disclosed by Step Finance on X, with security experts and analysts, including Hemendra Bisht, reporting on the suspicious transactions and providing updates. Step Finance took countermeasures and announced that it would review its security measures, including stricter audits and bug bounty programmes.

On 27 January 2026, the cybercrime group ShinyHunters reported that it had breached Panera Bread's systems, exposing approximately 14 million customer records, including names, email addresses, postal addresses, phone numbers, and account-related details, with the stolen information amounting to roughly 760 MB of compressed data. While security experts stated that there is no indication that financial or sensitive personal information was stolen, they warned that the types of data stolen could still be used for phishing campaigns and urged vigilance for potential victims.

On or around 22 January 2026, the Dresden State Art Collections ("SKD") in Germany were targeted by a cyberattack from unknown actors that compromised a large part of their digital infrastructure. The attackers disrupted the websites of the SKD and further disrupted telephone communications infrastructure; the SKD's online ticket sales and the online shop were also rendered inaccessible. A crisis team was set up with the Dresden police and the regional criminal police office to address the incident, and by 29 January 2026, the SKD's services were rendered fully accessible again.

Between 25 and 26 January 2026, the Vladimir Bread Factory, a major bread producer in Russia's Vladimir region, had its internal systems disrupted in a cyber incident from unknown actors, resulting in the compromise of the factory's internal digital systems, including office computers, servers, electronic document management tools, and the 1C enterprise accounting system. Although production was not affected and bakeries continued to operate at full capacity, the outage hindered order processing and deliveries, causing difficulties for local residents, retail outlets, and food suppliers for social institutions. The factory's staff shifted to a round-the-clock schedule and temporarily reverted to manual processing of orders and shipments to mitigate the disruption.

On 28 January 2026, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), in coordination with the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida and the Department of Justice's Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), seized the clearnet and dark web domains of RAMP (Ramp4u.io), a Russian-language cybercrime forum used by ransomware affiliates, malware developers, and initial access brokers. The seizure was confirmed by seizure banners visible on both domains, which redirected to notices with FBI and DOJ seals, and the nameservers were updated to reflect the seizure. A user known as Stallman, believed to be one of the RAMP operators or insiders, posted a statement on the underground forum XSS acknowledging that law enforcement had gained control of RAMP, expressing regret over the loss, and confirming that RAMP has been fully compromised and is no longer under his or the team's control.

On 28 January 2026, Kangwon National University Hospital was the victim of a ransomware attack by unknown actors, which resulted in the "entire computer network" of the hospital being rendered inoperable. According to reporting on the incident, the ransomware attack severely disrupted outpatient and inpatient care due to several medical imaging systems (MRIs and CTs) being completely inaccessible. This further resulted in delayed diagnoses for patients, according to media reporting. The incident followed a similar incident a day prior which occurred at another South Korean university hospital, Chonnam National University Hospital.

On 27 January 2026, Chungnam National University Hospital (CNUH) in South Korea was the victim of a ransomware attack by unknown actors, which resulted in imaging systems being temporarily disrupted. While initial reporting stated that the hospital had enacted a "swift response" and had mitigated data theft. Un unnamed actor listed Chungnam National University Hospital on an encrypted file uploading site, publishing information on technical infrastructure and promising "future updates" with client information.

Pakistan-linked threat actors conducted two cyberespionage campaigns, codenamed Gopher Strike and Sheet Attack, targeting Indian government entities in September 2025. Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the campaigns and assessed with medium confidence that the activity may originate from a new subgroup or a Pakistan-linked group operating in parallel to APT36. In the Gopher Strike campaign, the threat actors distributed spearphishing emails containing PDF documents with blurred images, prompting recipients to download a fake Adobe Acrobat update. The payload delivery infrastructure was configured to respond only to requests from IP addresses in India. The malicious ISO file contained GOGITTER, a Golang-based downloader that deployed GITSHELLPAD, a backdoor leveraging private GitHub repositories for command-and-control communication. Zscaler observed the threat actors issuing more than 200 post-compromise commands and deploying Cobalt Strike Beacon via GOSHELL, a Golang-based shellcode loader. Zscaler ThreatLabz published the findings on 26 January 2026.

On or around 26 January 2026, a ransomware attack disrupted the functioning of the Sanxenxo Town Council in Pontevedra. The town council's operators were unable to access the equipment at the Casa Consistorial for several hours. Two municipal companies, Nauta and Turismo de Sanxenxo, were not affected by the attack because they operate separate networks. The attackers demanded a ransom of around 5,000 dollars in bitcoins. The council did not agree to pay the ransom and filed a complaint with the Guardia Civil. The technical and security services resorted to daily backups to resolve the effects of the attack, and work was being done in coordination with the Centre of Cybersecurity Operations for Local Entities and the National Intelligence Centre to recover the information and return to normal operations.  The mayor, Telmo Martín, informed the public about the attack, stating that it would take longer than initially thought to resolve the issue.

On Sunday, 26 January 2026, Sundhed.dk, Denmark's central access to health records and test results, was hit by a DDoS attack, making the site inaccessible for several hours.
